title: Higher education is expanding faster than completion, equitable mobility, leadership access, and institutional AI readiness
source_unit: UNESCO IESALC, Higher education global trends report 2026: Towards inclusive, equitable and quality higher education in an internationally mobile landscape
geography: Global higher-education systems across 146 countries, with comparative enrollment, completion, financing, gender, mobility, refugee access, digitalization, and AI-policy evidence

denominator.unit: countries mapped through UNESCO Higher Education Policy Observatory and complementary resources

enrollment.unit: million students enrolled in higher education in 2024

enrollment_ratio.unit: percent global higher-education enrollment ratio in 2024

completion.unit: percent graduation ratio from bachelor’s and master’s programmes in 2024

completion_gap.value: completion has not kept pace with enrollment expansion

observations.method: Comparative analysis using the UNESCO Higher Education Policy Observatory, UNESCO Institute for Statistics, and literature across ten interconnected dimensions of higher education.
observations.uncertainty: Enrollment, graduation, and ratio measures have different denominators and timing; global aggregates can conceal large differences by country income, gender, field, institution, and student background.
observations.subgroup: Students and prospective students, institutions, academic staff, households financing participation, and countries with sharply different enrollment and completion capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Expansion can still improve opportunity even when completion lags; a low global graduation ratio does not establish that enrollment expansion caused lower completion or poor learning.

observations.period: 2000-2025; international student mobility and refugee access

denominator.unit: global internationally mobile student and refugee-access frame

mobility_growth.value: international student mobility more than tripled since 2000

mobility_reach.unit: percent or fewer of students globally benefiting from international mobility

refugee_enrollment.unit: percent refugee enrollment in higher education in 2025

recognition_barrier.value: recognition of qualifications remains a key barrier for refugee access

observations.method: Comparative reporting on international mobility, refugee participation, qualification recognition, and access across global higher-education systems.
observations.uncertainty: Mobility counts and refugee enrollment measures depend on definitions, country reporting, legal status, destination coverage, and the ability to recognize prior study; they do not measure student outcomes after access.
observations.subgroup: International students, refugees, displaced learners, origin and destination institutions, credential evaluators, families, and labor markets receiving graduates.
observations.counterinterpretation: Mobility is not the only route to quality or opportunity; domestic institutions, online learning, regional cooperation, and recognition reforms can widen access without physical international movement.

observations.period: 2024-2025; gender, academic leadership, and AI readiness

denominator.unit: global higher-education equity and institutional-policy frame

gender_enrollment.value: women outnumber men in higher education overall but remain underrepresented at doctoral level and in STEM fields

senior_leadership.unit: approximately percent of senior academic leadership roles held by women

national_ai_policies.unit: approximately percent of countries with national AI policies by 2024

institutional_ai_strategy.unit: percent or fewer of higher-education institutions with an AI strategy or formal AI policy in the report frame

observations.method: Comparative synthesis of higher-education participation, gender and leadership indicators, national AI policies, and institutional strategy reporting.
observations.uncertainty: Gender and AI-policy measures use different populations, years, and definitions; representation is not equivalent to authority, policy implementation, or educational quality.
observations.subgroup: Women students, doctoral candidates, STEM learners, academic leaders, faculty, institutions, national ministries, and communities affected by university AI deployment.
observations.counterinterpretation: A formal AI strategy is only one indicator of readiness; institutions may have active practices without a standalone policy, while a policy may exist without resources or effective implementation.

public_investment.unit: percent of global GDP invested in tertiary education

income_gradient.value: tertiary-education investment ranges from 0.3% of GDP in low-income countries to 1.5% in high-income countries

tuition_free_mandate.unit: percent of countries with a tuition-free mandate

public_scholarships.unit: percent of countries offering publicly funded scholarships

observations.method: Comparative analysis of public expenditure, tuition policy, scholarship provision, and system resources across higher-education systems.
observations.uncertainty: Spending and policy indicators do not establish per-student adequacy, distribution, quality, household costs, debt, or whether tuition-free mandates are fully implemented.
observations.subgroup: Students and households facing tuition, housing, transport, and textbook costs; public universities, governments, donors, and labor markets depending on tertiary skills.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher spending does not guarantee access or quality; targeted scholarships, student supports, institutional efficiency, and labor-market alignment may matter as much as aggregate expenditure.

related_sources.claim: UNESCO Higher Education Policy Observatory launch note with country coverage, completion, mobility, gender, refugee, finance, and AI-policy findings.
Official UNESCO IESALC publication page and report downloads.

boundary: This record adds a higher-education, mobility, equity, finance, labor-market, and institutional-AI-readiness route. It uses aggregate comparative public data and report synthesis, not respondent-level ingestion, student transcripts, causal estimates of higher-education returns, a ranking of institutions, or proof that enrollment expansion translates into completion, quality, or mobility for every group.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNESCO IESALC report page and Higher Education Policy Observatory launch note reviewed for global enrollment, completion, mobility, refugee access, gender and leadership, finance, and AI-policy indicators.
